titolo: Why Did the Dutch Rule Indonesia for 350 Years but Leave No Dutch?

numero.sotto: SPOKE DUTCH AT THE END OF RULE

descrizione:
Indonesia has more than 280 million people, and many say they were ruled by the Dutch for 350 years. So why does almost nobody there speak Dutch? Spain left Spanish across Latin America, Britain left English, France left French. The Dutch left almost nothing.

We follow the story from the spice company VOC and the founding of Batavia, through the Malay language, the elite Dutch schools, the 1928 Youth Pledge and the Japanese occupation, to the 5,000 Dutch words that still live inside Indonesian today.

scene.testo: Almost 300 years of Dutch rule on Java. Not one word kept. A company that wanted only money, a pledge in 1928, and one big question: why?
Nearly 42 million people live in the city they built. So why does hardly anyone there speak their language?
Indonesia has more than 280 million people, and many will tell you they were colonized by the Dutch for 350 years. Kids learn it at school.

eventi.testo: 350 years of Dutch rule, they say

scene.testo: So you would expect plenty of Dutch to have stuck. Spain left Spanish across Latin America. Britain left English everywhere. France left French across half of Africa.
But Dutch in Indonesia is a memory for a few elderly people, plus some historians and lawyers who need it to read old records.

eventi.testo: Dutch survives only in old records

scene.testo: Even near the end of Dutch rule, only about one person in a hundred spoke any of it.
My wife's mother was born in Palembang on Sumatra. Her family out there is more than 50 people, and not one speaks a word of Dutch.

eventi.testo: Zero Dutch speakers in the family

scene.testo: Many of them do speak decent English. And last time, in the Philippines, Spain stayed 333 years and Spanish never really caught on. Next to Indonesia, that looks like a success.
Digging in, I found the Dutch mostly never tried to spread their language. For a long time, many were happy to keep it that way.
First, that 350 years. It runs from 1596, when the first Dutch ships reached Java, to independence in 1945.
In 1968, historian G.J. Resink studied old treaties and argued that much of Indonesia stayed independent for most of that time.
Aceh, at the northern tip of Sumatra, was not conquered until 1903. The kingdom of Klungkung on Bali held out until 1908.
So plenty of Indonesians lived under the Dutch for a few decades at most. That is part of the answer, but it does not explain Java.
The Dutch ran parts of Java for well over 300 years, and Dutch never took hold there either. To see why, look at who actually showed up.
In 1602, the Dutch merged their spice firms into one giant company, the VOC. The government gave it a monopoly on Dutch trade in Asia.
In 1619, Governor-General Jan Pieterszoon Coen attacked Jayakarta, drove out the Banten troops, and built a new town on the ruins.

eventi.descrizione: 17th-century Dutch governor-general, black hat, stern face

scene.testo: Coen wanted to call it New Hoorn, after his hometown. His bosses picked Batavia instead. Today it is Jakarta, the capital of Indonesia.
And a fun fact: with nearly 42 million people in its urban area, it is now the most populous city on Earth.
The VOC was there for profit: spices, safe ports, and as little trouble as possible. Making people Dutch would have cost a lot and earned nothing.
And it did not need to. The islands already shared a trade language: Malay.

eventi.testo: Malay was already the trade language

scene.testo: For centuries, Arab, Indian, Chinese and local merchants used it to do business from Sumatra all the way to the Spice Islands.

eventi.testo: Malay linked Sumatra to Spice Islands

scene.testo: It is an old language, too. The oldest dated Malay writing is on a stone from the year 683, found in Palembang.
So the Dutch learned Malay. It was far cheaper for company staff to pick up Malay than to teach millions of people Dutch.
You can see how tunnel-visioned they were: money, money, and more money. Even inside Batavia, Dutch struggled to get a look in.
The company brought enslaved people to the city from across Asia. Many came from India and Sri Lanka, where the Portuguese had ruled for a century.
Many spoke a Portuguese Creole. A creole is a new language that people with no shared tongue build, usually from the language of whoever rules.

eventi.testo: A creole is a brand new language

scene.testo: Their kids grew up speaking it as a language of its own, mostly Portuguese words mixed with bits of local Asian languages.
Over time many were freed and became known as the Mardijkers, from a word meaning free people. Their Creole spread fast.
Dutch families spoke it at home, and the church preached in it. I love that the Dutch built an Asian capital where a rival's tongue filled the streets.
Through the 1700s and 1800s, Malay slowly pushed the Creole out. One village near Jakarta, Kampung Tugu, held on; its last fluent speaker died in 2012.
By 1800, the VOC was hopelessly in debt. The Dutch state shut it down and took over its territory.
The new colonial government kept the company's habits, including running things in Malay. Dutch schools existed, but few, mostly for European children and the sons of local aristocrats.

eventi.testo: Dutch schools for the elite only

scene.testo: In 1900, about 1,500 Indonesians attended European schools, compared with 13,000 European pupils, in a colony of tens of millions.
Teaching Dutch to everyone would have cost money, and some officials worried it would give people ideas.
Some Dutch people did not even like being spoken to in Dutch. In 1900, a young Javanese woman named Kartini wrote about it in her letters.

eventi.descrizione: young Javanese noblewoman, 1900, traditional kebaya, writing letters

scene.testo: She described an official who kept speaking Malay to a senior Javanese aristocrat who knew good Dutch. Another Dutchman told her natives ought not to know Dutch.
So Dutch stayed the language of the top. If you spoke it, you were European, or one of the few Indonesians let into that world.
Around 1900, things shifted. In 1899, a Dutch lawyer named Van Deventer wrote that the Netherlands owed the Indies a debt of honor.

eventi.testo: A 'debt of honor' after decades of profit

scene.testo: Two years later, Queen Wilhelmina told Parliament the Netherlands had a moral calling toward the people there. It became known as the Ethical Policy.

eventi.descrizione: young Dutch queen, 1901, crown, formal dress

scene.testo: One way to repay that debt was schools. In 1914, the Dutch opened a new primary school taught in Dutch, mostly for nobles' and officials' children.
By 1928, about 75,000 Indonesians had finished a Western-style primary school. A big jump, but tiny in a colony of about 60 million.
Here is a striking comparison: that is about one graduate for every 800 people. Dutch schooling only reached beyond a tiny elite from 1914, and it all stopped in 1942.
And some people it produced used Dutch to organize against the Dutch. In October 1928, young nationalists from across the islands met in Batavia.
Many groups there had Dutch names, like Jong Java, and many leaders came from Dutch schools. Most meetings were held in Dutch.
One speaker, Siti Sundari, gave her speech in Dutch, and someone translated it into Malay.

eventi.descrizione: young Indonesian woman, 1928, kebaya, speaking at a podium

eventi.testo: Speech in Dutch, translated to Malay

scene.testo: On the 28th, they made a pledge Indonesians still celebrate yearly: one motherland, one nation, and one language of unity, which they called Indonesian.
It was just Malay with a new name. The obvious alternative was Javanese, the language of nearly half the population.
But Javanese changes its words depending on whether you speak to someone above or below you, which makes it hard for outsiders. And it would have handed the biggest group even more power.
Malay was the first language of fewer than 5 percent of people, so it belonged to no single group. And because of trade, people everywhere already knew some.
Just before the pledge was read, a 25-year-old journalist, Wage Rudolf Supratman, stood up with his violin and played a song he had written.
He played only the tune, with no words, because Dutch authorities were watching. That song became Indonesia's national anthem.

eventi.testo: The tune became the national anthem

scene.testo: The Dutch were still in charge and could have carried on for decades. Then, in early 1942, Japan invaded.
Java was the last big prize, and about a week after the Japanese landed there, the Dutch surrendered.
The Japanese banned Dutch from public life. Within months, Indonesian took over schools, offices, and newspapers. Japan pushed its own language too, but almost nobody had time to learn it.
That created a problem: Indonesian lacked words for many modern things. Japan set up a language commission, and writer Sutan Takdir Alisjahbana did most of the work.

eventi.descrizione: Indonesian writer, 1940s, round glasses, formal suit

eventi.testo: A commission to modernize the language

scene.testo: By his own count, they invented about 7,000 new terms. He later called the occupation the most decisive moment in the development of Indonesian.
In just three years, Indonesian had to replace everything Dutch had done, and it managed it. On August 17, 1945, two days after Japan surrendered, Sukarno and Hatta declared independence.

eventi.descrizione: first president of Indonesia, black peci cap, white suit

scene.testo: The Dutch came back and spent four years trying to retake the colony, with talks, ceasefires, and two big military offensives.
They finally handed over sovereignty on December 27, 1949. Even then they kept Western New Guinea, and in 1957 that dispute boiled over.
Workers and soldiers seized Dutch businesses, which Indonesia then nationalized, and around 46,000 Dutch citizens were told to leave.
Even the spelling changed. Indonesian was once written with Dutch rules, so guru, meaning teacher, was spelled g, o, e, r, o, e. Reforms in 1947 and 1972 cleaned it up.
So spoken Dutch left with the Dutch, but it left a lot of itself behind. Indonesian borrowed more than 5,000 Dutch words, more than any other language.

eventi.testo: Most Dutch loanwords of any language

scene.testo: An office is a kantor, from kantoor. A towel is a handuk, from handdoek. And a fridge is a kulkas, from koelkast.
Car gears are persneling, from versnelling. A carrot is a wortel, exactly like Dutch. A cinema is a bioskop, and if something is free, it is gratis.
Some older Dutch words now sound old-fashioned, and new words tend to come from English. The law held on to Dutch even longer.
Indonesia's criminal code was a Dutch colonial law from 1918, and the government never settled on one official translation, so lawyers used competing versions.
It was only replaced on January 2, 2026, and parts of the Dutch Civil Code from 1848 are still in force today.
So, depending on which island you stand on, Dutch rule lasted anywhere from about 30 years to well over 300.
They ran the place in Malay because it was cheaper and kept Dutch for a small elite. Then that elite chose Malay as the language of a new country.
Almost by accident, the Dutch helped give more than 280 million people the language that holds their country together.

eventi.testo: The Dutch accidentally united a nation
